newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.S. Rwanda aid plane departure delayed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Rwanda aid plane departure delayed.

text.p: The United States air force said on Tuesday the departure of its first cargo plane bound for Kigali to help in the Rwandan refugee crisis had been delayed.
A U.S. military spokesman at the Rhein-Main air base said the aircraft was being loaded with equipment and prepared for a flight to Rwanda, but it was uncertain when the plane would leave.
The spokesman could not explain why the flight, earlier set to leave at 1900 GMT, had been delayed.
"The flight has not yet departed and it is not yet clear when the plane will leave," the spokesman said.

The C-17 aircraft was being loaded with equipment to allow U.S. forces to set up an air traffic control system for Kigali airport. Also being put on board was equipment needed to unload humanitarian supplies on subsequent flights.
The spokesman said: "There are no armed troops on the flight to clear the way."

A spokesman for the U.S. European Command in Stuttgart said aside from the flight originating in Frankfurt, there would be two other flights bound for central Africa from the United States. Two of the three flights were scheduled to stop at military bases in Spain.
The three flights were planned to bring air traffic control eqipment and other goods to airports in Kigali, Rwanda, Mombasa, Kenya and in Entebbe, Uganda.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry announced earlier on Tuesday in Washington that the flights would be sent to Africa with the equipment.
Perry also said on Tuesday that the United States had changed plans to send security troops to Zaire and instead would provide fewer than 1,000 military logistics personnel to aid refugees in Rwanda.

Perry said the situation in central Africa remained fluid and, while a Canadian-led multinational force would now operate chiefly in Rwanda, Washington was ready to send protective troops to Zaire if necessary.

The United States was one of the most reluctant volunteers to the U.N.-backed 10,000-strong multinational force whose mission was mainly to help the 1.2 million Rwandan and Burundian Hutus stranded in eastern Zaire by a month-long rebellion.
About 14 countries who committed troops to the force are due to review their plans in Germany on Thursday.
